claim: LOX2 transcript accumulation was 2% of WT levels in irLOX2 and hemi-irLOX2.

claim: LOX2 transcript accumulation was unaffected in irPI plants.
source: Headspace measurements from field- and glasshouse-grown plants detected a similar 80–100% reduction in GLV emissions from irLOX2 and hemi-irLOX2 plants compared to WT and irPI (field, N=3, p=0.024 for hemi-irLOX2 v irPI, p>0.05 for hemi-irLOX2 vs WT and irLOX2 vs irPI and WT, but p=0.939 for irPI vs WT in Scheffe post hoc tests following one-way ANOVA: F3,8=7.346, p=0.011; glasshouse, N=4: irLOX2 and hemi-irLOX2 below limit of detection, p=0.834 for t-test irPI vs WT) (Figure 3), and transcript accumulation of LOX2 was 2% of WT levels in irLOX2 and hemi-irLOX2 (N=5, p<0.001 in Scheffe post hoc tests following two-way ANOVAs on log2-transformed data with factors W+OS treatment and genotype: treatment F1,32=0.021, p=0.887; genotype F3,32=635.477, p<0.001) but unaffected in irPI (p>0.9 in Scheffe post hoc test vs WT) (Figure 3).

claim: The emission of (E)-α-bergamotene does not differ significantly among the lines used.

(2000) and normalized as a percentage of the internal standard peak: WT, 67.9±17.1%; irPI, 30.2±13.2%; irLOX2, 26.6±5.8%; hemi-irLOX2, 42.7±23.3%; ANOVA: F3,12=1.338, p=0.308).

claim: The transformation process itself does not affect plant fitness or competitive ability.

evidence: This is a control result supported by citation and data.

claim: No Geocoris spp. individuals were observed on the first-year plot through May 2010.
source: In 2010, we planted into a first-year plot. Although plants were infested with laboratory strain M. sexta larvae (N=51) and baited with M. sexta eggs (N=50) over a 2-week period in 2010 (Figure 4), no Geocoris spp. individuals were observed on this plot through May.
evidence: This is an observation from the 2010 field experiment.

claim: Geocoris spp. first arrived and began to predate Manduca spp. eggs on the older plot on June 9, 2010.
source: There were also no Geocoris spp. observed through May on a nearby, older plot: Geocoris spp. first arrived and began to predate Manduca spp. eggs on the older plot on June 9.
evidence: This is an observation from the 2010 field experiment.

claim: Geocoris spp. were observed in May 2011 prior to the first infestation on the older plot.
source: In 2011, we planted into the older plot, where we observed Geocoris spp. in May prior to the first infestation (M2, Figure 4).
evidence: This is an observation from the 2011 field experiment.

claim: During infestation M2, Geocoris spp. were allowed to associate all four plant genotypes with the presence of prey.
source: During infestation M2 (Figure 4), we allowed Geocoris spp. to associate all four plant genotypes with the presence of prey: we infested half of all plants with equal numbers of first-instar M. sexta larvae from the laboratory strain and, because Geocoris spp. predate more from GLV-emitting or-perfumed plants (Kessler and Baldwin, 2001; Halitschke et al., 2008; Allmann and Baldwin, 2010), we supplemented GLV emission from irLOX2 and hemi-irLOX2 plants by placing cotton swabs with lanolin paste containing GLVs representative of the M. sexta-fed N. attenuata headspace (Table 1 Allmann and Baldwin, 2010) adjacent to M. sexta-infested leaves.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: GLV emission from irLOX2 and hemi-irLOX2 plants was supplemented by placing cotton swabs with lanolin paste containing GLVs adjacent to M. sexta-infested leaves during M2.
source: During infestation M2 (Figure 4), we allowed Geocoris spp. to associate all four plant genotypes with the presence of prey: we infested half of all plants with equal numbers of first-instar M. sexta larvae from the laboratory strain and, because Geocoris spp. predate more from GLV-emitting or-perfumed plants (Kessler and Baldwin, 2001; Halitschke et al., 2008; Allmann and Baldwin, 2010), we supplemented GLV emission from irLOX2 and hemi-irLOX2 plants by placing cotton swabs with lanolin paste containing GLVs representative of the M. sexta-fed N. attenuata headspace (Table 1 Allmann and Baldwin, 2010) adjacent to M. sexta-infested leaves.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental manipulation.

claim: M. sexta larvae were predated at a rate of 12–37% over two 2- to 3-day trials during M2.
source: M. sexta larvae were predated at a rate of 12–37% over two 2- to 3-day trials.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the predation assays.

claim: Geocoris spp. tended to predate more larvae from GLV-supplemented plants during M2.
source: Geocoris spp. tended to predate more larvae from GLV-supplemented plants (Fisher's exact tests, 35–37% vs 22–27% May 5–6, N=59–60 larvae, p=0.066; 17–21% vs 12% May 13–15, N=92–100 larvae, p=0.069; combined trials, Bonferroni-corrected p=0.0063) (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the predation assays.

claim: Predation of both larvae and eggs without GLV supplementation was two to four times as great on GLV-emitting WT and irPI plants during M3.
source: Predation of both larvae and eggs without GLV supplementation was two to four times as great on GLV-emitting WT and irPI plants: 43%/60% (WT/irPI) for larvae and 34%/39% for eggs, vs 17%/33% (irLOX2/hemi-irLOX2) for larvae and 9%/20% for eggs (Fisher's exact tests: N=30 larvae, p=0.047 for irLOX2 vs WT, p=0.069 for hemi-irLOX2 vs irPI; N=88 eggs, p<0.001 for irLOX2 vs WT, p=0.013 for hemi-irLOX2 vs irPI) (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the predation assays.

claim: There was no difference among plant genotypes in the number of Geocoris spp. individuals during M3.
source: However, there was no difference among plant genotypes in the number of Geocoris spp. individuals (p>0.05 in Fisher's exact tests), indicating that Geocoris spp. regularly survey all plants and use GLVs as a short-distance cue to determine which plants harbor prey.
evidence: This is a result from Geocoris spp. counts.

claim: Geocoris spp. regularly survey all plants and use GLVs as a short-distance cue to determine which plants harbor prey.
source: However, there was no difference among plant genotypes in the number of Geocoris spp. individuals (p>0.05 in Fisher's exact tests), indicating that Geocoris spp. regularly survey all plants and use GLVs as a short-distance cue to determine which plants harbor prey.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Geocoris spp. count data.

claim: Over the following week after the beginning of M3, Geocoris spp. predated a total of 80% of larvae from WT and irPI vs 47% from irLOX2 and 67% from hemi-irLOX2.

Over the following week, Geocoris spp. predated a total of 80% of these larvae from WT and irPI vs 47% from irLOX2 (Fisher's exact test, p=0.015 vs WT) and 67% from hemi-irLOX2 (p=0.382 vs irPI).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from extended predation monitoring.

claim: Geocoris spp. had the same opportunity to locate M. sexta larvae and eggs on all genotypes, but consistently preferred to predate from GLV-supplemented or -emitting plants.
source: In summary, Geocoris spp. had the same opportunity to locate M. sexta larvae and eggs on all genotypes, but consistently preferred to predate from GLV-supplemented or -emitting plants.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the predation experiments.

evidence: This is a result from damage assessments.

claim: Only irPI plants suffered significantly less M. sexta damage in trials M2 and M3.

evidence: This is a result from damage assessments.

(Figures 4 and 6, statistics Table 3).

claim: The reduction in growth and reproduction of irLOX2 and hemi-irLOX2 was also apparent in plants not infested with M. sexta in 2011.

claim: The effect of M. sexta feeding on growth and reproduction was not significant for irLOX2 or irPI plants in either year.

evidence: This is a statistical result from the growth and reproduction data.

claim: The lack of significant M. sexta feeding effect on irPI plants may be due to reduced feeding damage resulting from a lack of TPI-induced compensatory feeding.

evidence: This is a speculation based on previous findings and current data.

source: Yet hemi-irLOX2 plants, despite strongly reduced GLVs, still suffered reduced growth and reproduction from Manduca spp. feeding: M. sexta feeding reduced flower production rates by about 50% in WT and by about 30% in hemi-irLOX2 plants in 2010, although the overall reduction was only significant in WT; and reduced bud production significantly for both WT and hemi-irLOX2 by 25–30% in 2011 (Figure 6, statistics Table 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the 2010 experiment.

claim: M. sexta feeding reduced bud production significantly for both WT and hemi-irLOX2 by 25–30% in 2011.
source: Yet hemi-irLOX2 plants, despite strongly reduced GLVs, still suffered reduced growth and reproduction from Manduca spp. feeding: M. sexta feeding reduced flower production rates by about 50% in WT and by about 30% in hemi-irLOX2 plants in 2010, although the overall reduction was only significant in WT; and reduced bud production significantly for both WT and hemi-irLOX2 by 25–30% in 2011 (Figure 6, statistics Table 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the 2011 experiment.

claim: All genotypes were attacked by mirid (Tupiocoris notatus) and noctuid herbivores which caused similar amounts of damage across genotypes and years.
source: All genotypes were attacked by mirid (Tupiocoris notatus) and noctuid herbivores which caused similar amounts of damage across genotypes and years (ca. 15% and 3% of total canopy area, respectively) although irLOX2 plants suffered 60% less mirid and noctuid damage by the end of M3 in 2011 (N=24–28; Bonferroni-corrected Kruskal-Wallis test, noctuids May 5, p=0.027, all pairwise tests Bonferroni-corrected p>0.05; one-way ANOVAs with factor genotype on arcsine-transformed data: mirids May 27, F3,103=5.291, p=0.002, p<0.05 for irLOX2 vs hemi-irLOX2 and irPI in Scheffe post hoc tests, noctuids May 27, F3,103=3.503, p=0.018, all post hoc tests p>0.05; all other comparisons p>0.05; Figures 4 and 7).
evidence: This is a result from herbivore damage monitoring.

claim: irLOX2 plants suffered 60% less mirid and noctuid damage by the end of M3 in 2011.

evidence: This is a quantitative result from herbivore damage monitoring.

claim: Reduced herbivore damage on irLOX2 in 2011 could have increased the growth and reproduction of irLOX2 plants relative to WT, but cannot explain why irLOX2 plants instead displayed reduced growth and reproduction.
source: Reduced herbivore damage on irLOX2 in 2011 could have increased the growth and reproduction of irLOX2 plants relative to WT, but cannot explain why irLOX2 plants instead displayed reduced growth and reproduction.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the damage and fitness data.

claim: Plants in 2011 were also damaged by flea beetles and grasshoppers (<3% of canopy area).
source: Plants in 2011 were also damaged by flea beetles and grasshoppers (<3% of canopy area, Kruskal-Wallis tests, N=24–28, all comparisons p>0.05, Figure 7).
evidence: This is a result from herbivore damage monitoring.

claim: Reduced growth and reproduction of uninfested irLOX2 and hemi-irLOX2 plants in 2011 might have been due to non-herbivory-related factors.

evidence: This is a speculation about alternative explanations.

claim: Assay M4 is the more robust basis for the argument that GLV-mediated indirect defense increases plant reproduction.
source: Because of this uncertainty, we conducted assay M4 (Figure 4) in which plants were carefully matched for size and prior reproduction (Figure 8), and this experiment is the more robust basis for our argument that GLV-mediated indirect defense increases plant reproduction.
evidence: This is a methodological justification by the authors.

claim: In both 2010 and 2011, triplets of WT, irPI and hemi-irLOX2 plants were selected that were similar in size, reproductive output, apparent health, and prior damage.

evidence: This is a description of the experimental design for M1 and M4.

claim: In the absence of Geocoris spp. in 2010, genotypes did not differ in M. sexta mortality or plant reproduction.
source: In the absence of Geocoris spp. in 2010, genotypes did not differ in M. sexta mortality (N=51 larvae)—which in every observed case was due to a failure of the larva to feed—or plant reproduction (N=17 plants) (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a result from the 2010 M1 experiment.

claim: M. sexta mortality in 2010 was in every observed case due to a failure of the larva to feed.
source: In the absence of Geocoris spp. in 2010, genotypes did not differ in M. sexta mortality (N=51 larvae)—which in every observed case was due to a failure of the larva to feed—or plant reproduction (N=17 plants) (Figure 9).
evidence: This is an observation about the cause of mortality in 2010.

claim: Flower removal itself does not cause a difference among genotypes.
source: This, and the fact that flower production did not differ among genotypes in 2011 through infestation M3 despite flower removal (Figure 6), indicates that flower removal itself does not cause a difference among genotypes, and suggests that the other differences among genotypes in growth and reproduction seen in 2011 (Figure 6, statistics Table 3) are real.
evidence: This is an inference from the flower removal control.

claim: The differences among genotypes in growth and reproduction seen in 2011 are real.
source: This, and the fact that flower production did not differ among genotypes in 2011 through infestation M3 despite flower removal (Figure 6), indicates that flower removal itself does not cause a difference among genotypes, and suggests that the other differences among genotypes in growth and reproduction seen in 2011 (Figure 6, statistics Table 3) are real.
evidence: This is an inference from the control experiments.

claim: In 2011, all reproductive meristems were removed from matched plants by cutting inflorescences at their base prior to M4.
source: In 2011, hemi-irLOX2, irPI and WT plants were matched prior to infestation M4 to exclude differences in growth, reproduction and Manduca spp. damage arising during M. sexta infestations M2 and M3 and from caged Manduca spp. during the egg predation assay (Figures 4, 7, and 8). Instead of regularly removing flowers, we removed all reproductive meristems from matched plants in 2011 by cutting inflorescences at their base.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure for M4.

claim: Removing reproductive meristems allowed following a new set of reproductive meristems through to seed set without incurring ripe seed.
source: This allowed us to follow a new set of reproductive meristems through to seed set without incurring ripe seed.
evidence: This is a justification for the meristem removal procedure.

claim: A similar number of reproductive meristems were cut from all plants in M4, and thus all plants were similarly affected by this cutting.
source: Because plants were matched prior to the assay, a similar number of reproductive meristems were cut from all plants, and thus all plants were similarly affected by this cutting (Figure 8, see 'Discussion').
evidence: This is a justification that the meristem removal did not bias the results.

claim: Oviposition by native Manduca spp. moths provided sufficient eggs prior to the beginning of M4.
source: Because oviposition by native Manduca spp. moths provided sufficient eggs prior to the beginning of M4 (Figure 4), we decided to conduct this infestation with wild larvae and thereby demonstrate that native larvae, like larvae of the lab strain, are susceptible to GLV-mediated predation.
evidence: This is an observation that allowed use of wild larvae.

claim: Native Manduca spp. larvae, like larvae of the lab strain, are susceptible to GLV-mediated predation.
source: Because oviposition by native Manduca spp. moths provided sufficient eggs prior to the beginning of M4 (Figure 4), we decided to conduct this infestation with wild larvae and thereby demonstrate that native larvae, like larvae of the lab strain, are susceptible to GLV-mediated predation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis tested in M4.

claim: One wild Manduca spp. neonate per plant was placed on a lower stem leaf to mimic natural oviposition rates in M4.
source: To make M4 a realistic test, we placed one wild Manduca spp. neonate per plant on a lower stem leaf to mimic natural oviposition rates (Kessler and Baldwin, 2001).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design for M4.

claim: During the first to third larval instars, wild Manduca spp. mortality was 38% on hemi-irLOX2 plants vs 62–76% on matched WT and irPI plants in M4.
source: During the first to third larval instars in which larvae are vulnerable to Geocoris spp. predation (Kessler and Baldwin, 2001), wild Manduca spp. mortality was 38% on hemi-irLOX2 plants vs 62–76% on matched WT and irPI plants; the overall mortality of larvae on all three lines was significantly different (N=21 larvae, Bonferroni-corrected pairwise comparisons by Friedman tests, p<0.01) (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the M4 experiment.

claim: The overall mortality of wild Manduca spp. larvae on all three lines was significantly different in M4.
source: During the first to third larval instars in which larvae are vulnerable to Geocoris spp. predation (Kessler and Baldwin, 2001), wild Manduca spp. mortality was 38% on hemi-irLOX2 plants vs 62–76% on matched WT and irPI plants; the overall mortality of larvae on all three lines was significantly different (N=21 larvae, Bonferroni-corrected pairwise comparisons by Friedman tests, p<0.01) (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the M4 experiment.

claim: Manduca spp. mortality on hemi-irLOX2 jumped to 70% in the fourth and semi-final larval instar.
source: Although Manduca spp. mortality on hemi-irLOX2 jumped to 70% in the fourth and semi-final larval instar, this was likely due to predation by whiptail lizards (Cnemidophorus spp.) which were present on the field plot: these lizards predate late-instar Manduca and are attracted to short-chain fatty-acid volatiles produced by the larvae due to ingestion of acyl sugars in plant trichomes (Stork et al., 2011; Weinhold and Baldwin, 2011).
evidence: This is an observation from the M4 experiment.

claim: The increased mortality on hemi-irLOX2 in the fourth instar was likely due to predation by whiptail lizards.
source: Although Manduca spp. mortality on hemi-irLOX2 jumped to 70% in the fourth and semi-final larval instar, this was likely due to predation by whiptail lizards (Cnemidophorus spp.) which were present on the field plot: these lizards predate late-instar Manduca and are attracted to short-chain fatty-acid volatiles produced by the larvae due to ingestion of acyl sugars in plant trichomes (Stork et al., 2011; Weinhold and Baldwin, 2011).
evidence: This is an inference based on observations and cited literature.

claim: Whiptail lizards predate late-instar Manduca and are attracted to short-chain fatty-acid volatiles produced by the larvae due to ingestion of acyl sugars in plant trichomes.
source: Although Manduca spp. mortality on hemi-irLOX2 jumped to 70% in the fourth and semi-final larval instar, this was likely due to predation by whiptail lizards (Cnemidophorus spp.) which were present on the field plot: these lizards predate late-instar Manduca and are attracted to short-chain fatty-acid volatiles produced by the larvae due to ingestion of acyl sugars in plant trichomes (Stork et al., 2011; Weinhold and Baldwin, 2011).
evidence: This is information from cited literature.

claim: The hemi-irLOX2 plants had produced 40–50% fewer buds and flowers than matched WT and irPI plants by the end of M4.
source: By the end of the assay, the hemi-irLOX2 plants had produced 40–50% fewer buds and flowers than matched WT and irPI plants (N=21 plants, p<0.05 in Scheffe post hoc tests for hemi-irLOX2 vs WT and irPI flowers and buds following a repeated-measures MANOVA over all flower and bud counts, Wilks' Lambda for the interaction of line and day: F12,110=2.835, p=0.002) (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the M4 experiment.

claim: The reduced bud and flower production in hemi-irLOX2 was not due to accelerated seed set.
source: This reduced bud and flower production was not due to accelerated seed set: unripe seed capsules on hemi-irLOX2 plants were also reduced by 50% (N=21 plants, p=0.021 for hemi-irLOX2 vs irPI in a Scheffe post hoc test following an ANOVA with genotype as the factor, F2,60=4.142, p=0.021) (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a result ruling out an alternative explanation.

claim: Herbivore-induced GLV emissions function as indirect defenses by increasing predation of Manduca spp. larvae twofold, resulting in a twofold increase in bud and flower production for N. attenuata in its native habitat.
source: These data demonstrate that herbivore-induced GLV emissions function as indirect defenses by increasing predation of Manduca spp. larvae twofold, resulting in a twofold increase in bud and flower production for N. attenuata in its native habitat.
evidence: This is the main conclusion from the M4 experiment.

claim: M. sexta and M. quinquemaculata did not differ in their growth or instar progression on plants in M4.
source: M. sexta and M. quinquemaculata did not differ in their growth or instar progression (N=11–13, repeated measures ANOVA for days 4–11, Wilks' Lambda for the interaction of day and species: F11,12=1.356, p=0.311).
evidence: This is a result from analysis of the two Manduca species.

claim: It is likely that mortality of M. sexta and M. quinquemaculata was equal prior to the third instar in M4.
source: Because larvae of the two species cannot be distinguished before the third instar, we could not test whether mortality was equal for both species in the first three instars; however, because other collections of wild eggs around the same time as the collection for our experiment yielded a 1:1 ratio of species, and because our ratio of the species remained 1:1 after larvae reached the third instar, it is likely that mortality of the two species was equal prior to the third instar.
evidence: This is an inference based on species ratios.

claim: TPIs had a less consistent and negative effect on Manduca spp. predation.
source: TPIs had a less consistent and, contrary to our expectations, negative effect on Manduca spp. predation (Figure 5); furthermore, there was no positive effect of TPIs on plant growth and reproduction (Figure 6, statistics Table 3) and only a marginal effect of TPIs on Manduca spp. growth under natural conditions (N=13–26 second instar larvae during M2, one-way ANOVAs with genotype as the factor, F3,77=2.792, p=0.046, all post hoc tests p>0.05, Figure 10; N=8 second instar larvae during M4, paired t-test between matched WT and irPI, p=0.052).
evidence: This is a summary of results regarding TPIs.

claim: There was no positive effect of TPIs on plant growth and reproduction.
source: TPIs had a less consistent and, contrary to our expectations, negative effect on Manduca spp. predation (Figure 5); furthermore, there was no positive effect of TPIs on plant growth and reproduction (Figure 6, statistics Table 3) and only a marginal effect of TPIs on Manduca spp. growth under natural conditions (N=13–26 second instar larvae during M2, one-way ANOVAs with genotype as the factor, F3,77=2.792, p=0.046, all post hoc tests p>0.05, Figure 10; N=8 second instar larvae during M4, paired t-test between matched WT and irPI, p=0.052).
evidence: This is a result from the fitness measurements.

claim: There was only a marginal effect of TPIs on Manduca spp. growth under natural conditions.
source: TPIs had a less consistent and, contrary to our expectations, negative effect on Manduca spp. predation (Figure 5); furthermore, there was no positive effect of TPIs on plant growth and reproduction (Figure 6, statistics Table 3) and only a marginal effect of TPIs on Manduca spp. growth under natural conditions (N=13–26 second instar larvae during M2, one-way ANOVAs with genotype as the factor, F3,77=2.792, p=0.046, all post hoc tests p>0.05, Figure 10; N=8 second instar larvae during M4, paired t-test between matched WT and irPI, p=0.052).
evidence: This is a result from larval growth measurements.

claim: Wild Manduca spp. larvae feeding on WT plants reacted more sluggishly to experimental provocation than size-matched larvae on irPI plants.
source: Indeed, wild Manduca spp. larvae feeding on WT plants (infestation M4, Figure 4) reacted more sluggishly to experimental provocation than size-matched larvae on irPI plants: they were 75% less likely to attack when lifted off of the leaf (N=5 second-instar larvae matched for size, p=0.035 in paired t-test) (Figure 10, Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This is a result from the on-plant behavioral assay.

claim: Wild Manduca spp. larvae on WT plants were 75% less likely to attack when lifted off of the leaf compared to larvae on irPI plants.
source: Indeed, wild Manduca spp. larvae feeding on WT plants (infestation M4, Figure 4) reacted more sluggishly to experimental provocation than size-matched larvae on irPI plants: they were 75% less likely to attack when lifted off of the leaf (N=5 second-instar larvae matched for size, p=0.035 in paired t-test) (Figure 10, Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the behavioral assay.

claim: Larvae fed on WT leaves were 50% less likely to successfully attack the insect pin in the off-plant assay.
source: Similarly to the on-plant assay, larvae fed on WT leaves were 50% less likely to successfully attack the insect pin, either when initially poked, or poked and lifted with the pin (N=20 first-instar larvae matched for size, p<0.05 in paired t-tests) (Figure 10).
evidence: This is a result from the off-plant behavioral assay.

claim: WT-fed larvae ceased to grow for at least 24 hr after simulated attack, while irPI-fed larvae continued to grow.
source: We also monitored recovery post-trial and found that WT-fed larvae ceased to grow for at least 24 hr after simulated attack, while irPI-fed larvae continued to grow (p=0.016 in Student's t-test); mortality did not differ (p=0.527 in Fisher's exact test) (Figure 10).
evidence: This is a result from the recovery monitoring after the behavioral assay.

claim: Mortality did not differ between WT-fed and irPI-fed larvae after simulated attack.
source: We also monitored recovery post-trial and found that WT-fed larvae ceased to grow for at least 24 hr after simulated attack, while irPI-fed larvae continued to grow (p=0.016 in Student's t-test); mortality did not differ (p=0.527 in Fisher's exact test) (Figure 10).
evidence: This is a result from the recovery monitoring.

claim: TPIs may support indirect defense by weakening the response of larvae to predator attack.
source: Thus TPIs did not increase plant reproduction under attack from Manduca spp. in nature, but may support indirect defense by weakening the response of larvae to predator attack.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the behavioral assays.

claim: The contradictory higher predation rates of Manduca spp. larvae from irPI than from WT plants might reflect Geocoris spp.'s feeding preference if irPI-fed larvae are more nutritious than WT-fed larvae.
source: The contradictory higher predation rates of Manduca spp. larvae from irPI than from WT plants (Figure 5) might reflect Geocoris spp.'s feeding preference, if irPI-fed larvae are more nutritious than WT-fed larvae (Kaplan and Thaler, 2011).
evidence: This is a speculation to explain an unexpected result.

claim: Herbivore-induced GLV emissions function as indirect defenses by increasing predation of Manduca spp. twofold, resulting in a twofold increase in bud and flower production for N. attenuata in its native habitat.
source: Our data demonstrate that herbivore-induced GLV emissions function as indirect defenses by increasing predation of Manduca spp. twofold, resulting in a twofold increase in bud and flower production for N. attenuata in its native habitat.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study stated in the Discussion.

claim: There was no positive effect of TPIs on plant growth and reproduction and no significant effect of TPIs on Manduca spp. growth under natural conditions.
source: In contrast, there was no positive effect of TPIs on plant growth and reproduction and no significant effect of TPIs on Manduca spp. growth under natural conditions; however, TPIs may support indirect defense by weakening the response of larvae to predator attack.
evidence: This is a summary of TPI results stated in the Discussion.

claim: TPIs may support indirect defense by weakening the response of larvae to predator attack.
source: In contrast, there was no positive effect of TPIs on plant growth and reproduction and no significant effect of TPIs on Manduca spp. growth under natural conditions; however, TPIs may support indirect defense by weakening the response of larvae to predator attack.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the behavioral data stated in the Discussion.

claim: The tendency towards higher predation rates from irPI than from WT plants could reflect Geocoris spp.'s preference if irPI-fed larvae are more nutritious than WT-fed larvae.
source: Although this indicates that predation rates from irPI plants should be reduced, we observed a tendency towards higher predation rates from irPI than from WT plants; this could reflect Geocoris spp.'s preference if irPI-fed larvae are more nutritious than WT-fed larvae (Kaplan and Thaler, 2011).
evidence: This is a speculation to explain an unexpected result stated in the Discussion.

claim: Functional RNAi constructs may be rendered ineffective as a result of insufficient gene dosage when present in the hemizygous state.
source: It is common molecular biology knowledge that functional RNAi constructs may be rendered ineffective as a result of insufficient gene dosage, for example, Travella et al. (2006) and references therein, which may occur when an RNAi construct is present in the hemizygous state (García-Pérez et al., 2004).
evidence: This is an explanation for the inactivity of the irPI construct in hemi-irLOX2 plants, supported by citations.

claim: The 35S promoter which drives the transcription of the RNAi construct may be methylated, an epigenetic effect which can reduce the dose of RNAi in individual plants within a single transformed line.
source: The 35S promoter which drives the transcription of the RNAi construct may also be methylated: an epigenetic effect which can reduce the dose of RNAi in individual plants within a single transformed line (A Weinhold, unpublished data).
evidence: This is an alternative explanation for construct inactivity.

claim: For field-grown N. attenuata plants, fewer than 5% of buds and flowers (in total) are aborted by healthy plants.
source: For field-grown N. attenuata plants, fewer than 5% of buds and flowers (in total) are aborted by healthy (not diseased) plants, and abortion seems always to be due to damage by insects (M C Schuman and I T Baldwin, personal observation, June 2010).
evidence: This is an observation from the field supporting the use of buds and flowers as fitness proxies.

claim: More than 70% of seed set from plants in native N. attenuata populations results from fertilization via self-pollen.
source: Plants are self-compatible and more than 70% of seed set from plants in native populations results from fertilization via self-pollen (Sime and Baldwin, 2003).
evidence: This is a characteristic of N. attenuata reproduction supported by citation.

claim: Numbers of buds and flowers correlate to lifetime seed capsule production, which in turn correlates to lifetime seed production.
source: Thus numbers of buds and flowers correlate to lifetime seed capsule production, which in turn correlates to lifetime seed production, which has been used as a proxy measure of Darwinian fitness (Baldwin, 1998; van Loon et al., 2000; Hoballah and Turlings, 2001).
evidence: This is a justification for using buds and flowers as fitness measures, supported by citations.

claim: The transgenic lines used do not vary in seed mass or their seedling viability under laboratory conditions.
source: The transgenic lines used do not vary in seed mass or their seedling viability under laboratory conditions.
evidence: This is a control observation supporting the validity of fitness comparisons.

claim: The hemi-irLOX2 plants chosen in 2011 had produced more flowers than WT – but not more than irPI—prior to the start of infestation M4.
source: The hemi-irLOX2 plants chosen in 2011 had produced more flowers than WT – but not more than irPI—prior to the start of infestation M4 (Figures 4 and 8).
evidence: This is an observation about the matched plants used in M4.

claim: The number of inflorescences cut and the number of side branches did not differ for the plants chosen for M4.
source: This did not correspond to more cuts on average for hemi-irLOX2 when removing reproductive meristems: meristems were cut at the bases of inflorescences which contained mostly buds, and the number of these did not differ for the plants chosen, nor did the number of side branches (Figure 8) which bore most reproductive meristems.
evidence: This is a justification that meristem removal was equivalent across genotypes.

claim: In the absence of additional effects during infestation M4, the reproduction of the matched hemi-irLOX2 plants should have been similar to that of WT and irPI.
source: Therefore, in the absence of additional effects during infestation M4, the reproduction of the matched hemi-irLOX2 plants should have been similar to that of WT and irPI.
evidence: This is a logical expectation based on the matching procedure.

claim: These data set the stage for the use of HIPVs as part of integrated pest management strategies (IPM).
source: By indicating the long-sought indirect defensive function of HIPVs, these data set the stage for the use of HIPVs as part of integrated pest management strategies (IPM), which rely in part on recruiting biological control agents to reduce pesticide use (Horne and Page, 2008).
evidence: This is a practical implication of the findings.

claim: IPM strategies rely in part on recruiting biological control agents to reduce pesticide use.
source: By indicating the long-sought indirect defensive function of HIPVs, these data set the stage for the use of HIPVs as part of integrated pest management strategies (IPM), which rely in part on recruiting biological control agents to reduce pesticide use (Horne and Page, 2008).
evidence: This is a characteristic of IPM supported by citation.

claim: Biological control agents used in IPM are usually naturally occurring generalist parasitoids and predators, such as Geocoris spp.
source: These agents are usually naturally occurring generalist parasitoids and predators, such as Geocoris spp. (Eubanks and Denno, 1999, 2000; Allison and Hare, 2009; Allmann and Baldwin, 2010).
evidence: This is information about IPM agents supported by citations.

claim: HIPVs are produced by genotypes of most, if not all crop plants.
source: HIPVs are produced by genotypes of most, if not all crop plants and IPM would benefit from selective breeding or engineering of HIPV emission (Kos et al., 2009) rather than relying on alternatives such as controlled release dispensers, which have mixed success and require large amounts of synthetic HIPVs (Kaplan, 2012).
evidence: This is a general statement about HIPV production in crops.

claim: IPM would benefit from selective breeding or engineering of HIPV emission.
source: HIPVs are produced by genotypes of most, if not all crop plants and IPM would benefit from selective breeding or engineering of HIPV emission (Kos et al., 2009) rather than relying on alternatives such as controlled release dispensers, which have mixed success and require large amounts of synthetic HIPVs (Kaplan, 2012).
evidence: This is a recommendation supported by citation.

claim: Controlled release dispensers for HIPVs have mixed success and require large amounts of synthetic HIPVs.
source: HIPVs are produced by genotypes of most, if not all crop plants and IPM would benefit from selective breeding or engineering of HIPV emission (Kos et al., 2009) rather than relying on alternatives such as controlled release dispensers, which have mixed success and require large amounts of synthetic HIPVs (Kaplan, 2012).
evidence: This is a limitation of an alternative approach supported by citation.

claim: PIs may be employed to enhance the efficiency of indirect defense, especially combined with toxins like Bt.
source: PIs may be employed to enhance the efficiency of indirect defense, especially combined with toxins like Bt that directly target herbivores and are safe for biological control agents.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the study findings.

claim: Bt toxins directly target herbivores and are safe for biological control agents.
source: PIs may be employed to enhance the efficiency of indirect defense, especially combined with toxins like Bt that directly target herbivores and are safe for biological control agents.
evidence: This is a characteristic of Bt toxins.

claim: There are growing concerns about field-evolved Bt resistance.
source: With growing concerns about field-evolved Bt resistance (Liu et al., 2010), indirect defenses promise an effective 'first line of defense' against agricultural pests, to which not even specialist herbivores are likely to rapidly evolve resistance.
evidence: This is a current concern in agriculture supported by citation.

claim: Indirect defenses promise an effective 'first line of defense' against agricultural pests, to which not even specialist herbivores are likely to rapidly evolve resistance.
source: With growing concerns about field-evolved Bt resistance (Liu et al., 2010), indirect defenses promise an effective 'first line of defense' against agricultural pests, to which not even specialist herbivores are likely to rapidly evolve resistance.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the potential of indirect defenses.
